claims.text: The target alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has a homogeneous, distorted BCC or similar solid-solution matrix.
Intrinsic lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr favors spontaneous or engineered formation of coherent nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates develop within the distorted matrix of equimolar WTaTiVZr.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
The coherent precipitates act as internal dislocation channels or shearable barriers.
The coherent precipitates promote both dislocation glide and dislocation climb at high temperature.
Coherent precipitate interfaces relieve local stress concentrations that would otherwise promote premature crack initiation.
Stress-concentration relief by coherent precipitates delays brittle-crack initiation in WTaTiVZr.
Under comparable high-temperature loading, pure tungsten has limited dislocation mobility and tends toward brittle fracture.
Relative to pure tungsten, equimolar WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain or tensile ductility.
Relative to pure tungsten, equimolar WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater high-temperature fracture toughness.
Relative to pure tungsten, equimolar WTaTiVZr will show delayed crack initiation under high-temperature loading.
Relative to pure tungsten, equimolar WTaTiVZr will have enhanced resistance to creep deformation.
The proposed mechanism is applicable above approximately 1000 K and at strain rates permitting creep and plastic flow.
The benefit will diminish if coherent precipitate stability is compromised by extreme thermal shock.
The benefit will diminish in highly oxidizing environments.
The extent of coherent nanoprecipitate formation depends on processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the precipitates facilitate dislocation climb, while the predicted outcome includes enhanced creep resistance. Because climb commonly contributes to high-temperature creep, the hypothesis does not explain how promoting climb would reduce creep rate rather than accelerate it.
